# Count Objects Instead of Sanitizers

**Decision.** The C++ tests in
[[programming-fundamentals-and-oop-laboratories]] use an instrumented tracked payload to
assert ownership lifetimes in the portable baseline suite. AddressSanitizer and Undefined
Behavior Sanitizer remain an opt-in CMake configuration, not a prerequisite for the tests.

## Make the lifecycle observable

The tracked header supplies a payload whose construction and destruction update shared counters.
A test can reset a tracking_scope, exercise an ownership operation, and assert the expected
number of live, constructed, and destroyed objects. The project's small test harness then
reports those ordinary assertions through CTest like its other behavioural checks.

~~~cpp
tracking_scope scope;
// exercise an owning_ptr or tree operation
CHECK_EQ(tracked::alive, 0u);
~~~

This keeps the test's observation in standard C++ code. A supported compiler and CMake are
enough to run it; the README therefore presents the lifetime assertions as part of the regular
C++20 suite.

## A deliberately bounded signal

The counters answer a specific question: did this test path create and release the tracked
objects according to the ownership contract? They do not diagnose every memory-safety property.
They cannot replace runtime instrumentation for untracked allocations, buffer bounds,
use-after-free, or undefined behaviour that prevents the process from continuing.

The helper also records a repeated destructor observation through its marker, but
instrumentation does not make undefined behaviour safe. Tests should treat the counters as a
direct contract check, not as a general memory debugger.

## Why sanitizers stay available

Sanitizers provide a different kind of evidence and are valuable when the selected toolchain
supports them. The CMake option FUNDAMENTALS_SANITIZE enables that additional run without making
the repository's normal test command depend on a sanitizer runtime.

The two approaches are complementary: object counts make expected ownership transitions
assertable in every regular test run, while sanitizers can inspect a wider set of runtime
conditions in an environment configured for them.
